lead: This unit explains how a VR or AR system finds out what the user is doing: which control was pressed, where the hand is, which way the head has turned. After it you can pick an input device for a given 3D task, read a tracker's specification sheet, and explain how a headset keeps its pose steady.
about: Unit 2 is about the input side of a VR or AR system. Chapter 2.1 sets out the vocabulary — degrees of freedom, isotonic and isometric devices, latency, resolution — and applies it to the mouse, keyboard and 3D mouse on a desk. Chapter 2.2 goes to the trackers that report 3D position and orientation, and Chapter 2.3 shows how a tracked pose becomes navigation through a scene and manipulation of an object. Chapter 2.4 covers gesture interfaces and data gloves. Chapter 2.5 extends hand tracking to the whole body through motion capture. Chapter 2.6 lists the sensors behind all of this, with the noise and drift each one brings. Chapter 2.7, taught in only a few universities, closes on head tracking, yaw-pitch-roll, drift and the lighthouse approach.

chapters.idea: An input device is judged by its degrees of freedom, its mapping to the task and the feedback it gives, and desktop devices are the baseline every VR device is compared against.
chapters.depth: Define an input device for a 3D interface. Cover the characteristics used to compare devices: degrees of freedom (DOF, the number of independent motions reported); isotonic (moves with the hand), isometric (feels force but hardly moves) and elastic devices; absolute versus relative reporting; position control versus rate control; order of control; resolution, accuracy, precision and repeatability; latency, update rate and jitter; workspace; proprioception; fatigue; cost. Then the desktop devices: mouse, trackball, touchpad, joystick, spaceball, keyboard and touchscreen, plus 3D mice such as the 6-DOF puck, which some syllabi call special purpose input devices. End with a selection procedure: task first, then DOF, then control type, then feedback.

figure.title: Choosing an input device
figure.aria: Flowchart that starts from the user's task and narrows down through three questions to a chosen input device.

chapters.example: A VR cricket game runs at 60 frames per second, one frame every 16.7 ms. The bat tracker samples at 120 Hz. (a) How many tracker samples arrive per frame? (b) The menu cursor is a mouse with 800 counts per inch; the user moves it 1.5 inches. How many counts is that? (c) How many DOF must the bat tracker report? Answer: (a) 16.7 ms = 0.0167 s, so 120 × 0.0167 = 2.0, that is 2 samples per frame. (b) 800 × 1.5 = 1200 counts. (c) 6 DOF, three of position and three of orientation, because both the bat's position and its swing angle matter.
chapters.trap: DOF counts independent motions, not buttons or sensors. A mouse has 2 DOF of motion and three buttons; a 6-DOF puck has 6 DOF and often no useful button. A mouse also reports relative movement, so it has no absolute position to feed a tracker.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, for where input sits among the components of a VR system.
chapters.leave: Output devices and haptics to Unit 3; travel, menus and usability testing to Unit 5; AR-specific input to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A 3D position tracker reports the position and orientation of a sensor in a fixed frame, and each tracker family trades workspace, accuracy, latency and immunity to interference differently.
chapters.depth: Define a tracker: a device that reports the pose of a sensor in a fixed reference frame at a stated rate. Cover the families. Mechanical: a linked arm, where joint angles give the pose. Magnetic: transmitter coils with a receiver, AC and DC forms, disturbed by steel and by CRT monitors. Ultrasonic: time of flight between emitters and microphones, then triangulation. Optical: markers or LEDs seen by cameras, outside-in and inside-out. Inertial: gyroscope for rate, accelerometer for gravity, dead reckoning and drift. Hybrid: usually optical plus inertial. For each give what it measures, its workspace, the order of its accuracy, its latency, what disturbs it, and whether it is tethered. Some syllabi say types of trackers and count only mechanical, magnetic, ultrasonic and optical.

figure.aria: Tree of the six tracker families under one root labelled 3D position trackers, each branch noting the physical quantity it uses.

chapters.example: An ultrasonic tracker measures a time of flight of 2.9 ms from an emitter to a microphone. The speed of sound in air at 20 °C is 343 m/s. (a) What distance does that give? (b) Three such distances from three fixed emitters give the position; if each distance carries a 1 mm error, what order of position error follows? (c) The room warms to 30 °C, where the speed of sound is 349 m/s. What distance does the same 2.9 ms now report? Answer: (a) 343 × 0.0029 = 0.995 m, about 1.00 m. (b) about 1 mm, since each distance error maps almost directly onto a position error. (c) 349 × 0.0029 = 1.012 m, roughly 17 mm longer, with nothing physical having moved.
chapters.trap: Resolution is not accuracy, and a fine resolution figure says nothing about systematic error. Also an ultrasonic distance depends on the speed of sound, so a warm room looks like a moved sensor.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for DOF, resolution, accuracy and latency; Unit 4 for the transforms that turn tracker readings into poses.
chapters.leave: Head tracking detail to 2.7; marker-based AR tracking and SLAM to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Navigation moves the viewpoint and manipulation moves objects, and both are built from a small set of techniques chosen to match distance, precision and the display.
chapters.depth: Split navigation into travel (moving the viewpoint) and wayfinding (knowing where you are). List travel techniques with their mechanism and one parameter each: physical walking, steering, teleport, fly, point-and-fly, and World-in-Miniature. Then manipulation: selection by ray casting, occlusion, Go-Go, aperture and sticky finger; manipulation by direct hand, HOMER, Scaled-World Grab and the voodoo doll. Then system control through 3D menus, gestures and speech, kept light because travel and menus return in Unit 5. Say where each technique fails: far objects, small objects, occluded objects, and fatigue over a long session. Some syllabi call this navigation and manipulation interfaces, or pair it with gesture interfaces.

figure.title: Go-Go reach mapping
figure.aria: Block diagram of the Go-Go mapping: hand distance is compared with a threshold, and only past it is a gain applied to reach further.

chapters.example: Go-Go maps physical hand distance d to virtual distance. Below the threshold D = 0.25 m the mapping is one to one; above it the gain is k = 2. (a) Find the virtual distance when d = 0.15 m. (b) When d = 0.40 m. (c) When d = 0.80 m. (d) A shelf sits 2 m away in the virtual room; what physical reach does the user need? Answer: (a) 0.15 m, below the threshold. (b) 0.25 + 2(0.40 − 0.25) = 0.55 m. (c) 0.25 + 2(0.80 − 0.25) = 1.35 m. (d) 0.25 + 2(d − 0.25) = 2 gives d = 1.125 m, still an uncomfortable stretch, which is why Go-Go alone is not used for very distant targets.
chapters.trap: Ray casting selects the first object along the ray, so it cannot pick an object hidden behind another. And Go-Go is linear below the threshold, so d must not be plugged into the gain formula when d < D.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for the tracked hand pose; Unit 1 for interaction among the three I's.
chapters.leave: Travel, wayfinding, menus and interface evaluation in depth to Unit 5; force feedback during manipulation to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A gesture interface turns hand shape and hand motion into commands without a button, and a data glove is the sensor that measures hand shape directly.
chapters.depth: Define a gesture interface. Cover the taxonomy: static posture versus dynamic gesture, contact versus non-contact, and symbolic, deictic and manipulative gestures. Then gesture input devices: data gloves with flex, fibre-optic or resistive-ink bend sensors; pinch gloves with contact sensors; 6-DOF wands with buttons; bare-hand camera tracking; and armband EMG. Give the recognition pipeline: sense, segment, extract features, classify by template matching, dynamic time warping, hidden Markov model or a small neural net, then apply hysteresis and a confidence threshold. Close with glove specifications: sensor count, resolution, sample rate, per-user calibration, repeatability, and the reasons a glove becomes uncomfortable over a long session. Some syllabi say types of gesture input devices, or digital glove.

figure.title: Data glove to gesture event
figure.aria: Pipeline that carries bend readings from glove sensors through digitising, calibration and classification to a single gesture event.

chapters.example: A data glove has 10 flex sensors, each read by an 8-bit ADC over a bend range of 0° to 180°, and it samples at 100 Hz. (a) What is the bend resolution in degrees per count? (b) How many bytes per second does the raw stream carry, counting one byte per sensor? (c) How many samples fall inside a 2-second calibration pose? (d) The fist threshold is 140° and the sensor jitters by ±3°. What goes wrong? Answer: (a) 180 ÷ 256 = 0.70° per count. (b) 10 × 100 = 1000 bytes per second. (c) 100 × 2 = 200 samples. (d) at 140° the jitter swings the reading across the threshold, so the gesture fires repeatedly; enter at 143° and leave at 137° instead.
chapters.trap: Do not count flex sensors as hand DOF: a 10-sensor glove does not give 10 independent joint angles, because finger joints are coupled. And a single threshold without hysteresis makes a held gesture repeat.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for 6-DOF tracking of the hand; Chapter 2.3 for selection, which gestures often replace.
chapters.leave: Speech and menu system control to Unit 5; haptic feedback inside a glove to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Body and hand tracking rebuild a skeleton from sensor data, and motion capture turns the recorded joint motion into animation.
chapters.depth: Cover body tracking: a joint hierarchy, a T-pose calibration, forward kinematics for the avatar and inverse kinematics to fit the measured points, plus occlusion and the capture volume. Then motion capture families: optical with passive retro-reflective markers, optical with active LEDs, markerless video-based capture, magnetic, mechanical exoskeleton and inertial suits; give frame rate, marker count, volume and the clean-up cost of each. Then hand tracking: glove versus camera, the 21-joint hand model, and why fingers occlude each other. Then the uses: animation, live performance, sports biomechanics, VR avatars, and face capture in one line. Some syllabi call this movement capture or video-based input.

figure.title: Optical motion capture
figure.aria: Pipeline from markers on a suit through a ring of cameras and triangulation to a fitted skeleton that yields joint angles.

chapters.example: An optical motion capture stage uses 12 cameras at 120 frames per second and 40 markers on the actor. A 10-second take is recorded. (a) How many marker samples are there? (b) Each sample is three coordinates stored as 4-byte floats; what is the raw data size? (c) The actor turns and one camera loses 5 markers for 0.5 s; how many marker samples are lost? Answer: (a) 40 × 120 × 10 = 48,000 marker samples. (b) 48,000 × 3 × 4 = 576,000 bytes, about 576 kB. (c) 5 × 120 × 0.5 = 300 samples.
chapters.trap: Markers give positions, not joint angles; the skeleton fit is a separate step that produces angles. And a lost marker is not a lost limb: the solver interpolates across the gap and can invent motion that never happened.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for hand tracking; Unit 4 for the kinematic chain and joint hierarchy.
chapters.leave: Face cloning and face motion analysis, where they are taught, elsewhere; character behaviour modelling to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: VR and AR systems infer the user's state and the shape of the world from sensors, and each sensor measures one physical quantity with its own noise, bias and drift.
chapters.depth: Group sensors by the quantity they measure. Inertial: accelerometer (specific force, gravity included), gyroscope (angular rate, with bias), magnetometer (magnetic heading, disturbed by steel and motors). Explain dead reckoning and why drift grows, with one line on complementary or Kalman fusion. Optical: RGB and IR cameras, with rolling shutter and exposure as error sources. Depth: structured light, time of flight and stereo. Environmental and body sensors: capacitive touch, flex, force and pressure, temperature, EMG, plus gaze tracking by pupil-centre corneal reflection. For each give what it measures, its unit, its main error, and where it sits in a headset or a phone. Leave marker and markerless AR tracking and SLAM to Unit 6.

figure.aria: Tree grouping XR sensors into inertial, camera, depth, environmental and physiological families, each with the quantity it measures.

chapters.example: A headset at rest reads a_z = 8.50 m/s² on the axis pointing up, with g = 9.81 m/s². (a) What tilt angle does that imply? (b) The gyroscope has a bias of 0.5° per second. How far does the integrated angle drift in 60 s? (c) A magnetometer heading is off by 10° because of a steel desk nearby; what happens to that error over time? Answer: (a) cos θ = 8.50 ÷ 9.81 = 0.866, so θ = 30.0°. (b) 0.5 × 60 = 30°. (c) it stays at 10°, because the magnetometer gives an absolute heading and nothing is integrated, so the error does not grow.
chapters.trap: A stationary accelerometer does not read zero; it reads g pointing up. And gyroscope bias error grows with time, while accelerometer and magnetometer errors do not.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for the trackers built from these sensors.
chapters.leave: Marker-based and markerless AR tracking, SLAM, and sensor-fusion algorithms in detail to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Head tracking turns gyroscope rates and the gravity vector into yaw, pitch and roll of the head, and drift plus the lighthouse approach show how a headset keeps that pose stable.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Cover 3-DOF orientation versus 6-DOF pose; yaw, pitch and roll with one stated sign convention; tilt from the gravity vector; drift from integrating gyroscope bias, and why gravity can correct pitch and roll but never yaw; heading correction from a magnetometer or a camera; prediction to hide latency; inside-out versus outside-in tracking. Then the lighthouse approach: two base stations sweep narrow IR beams across the room, photodiodes on the headset timestamp each hit, the timing of the sweep gives the angle to that station, and angles from both stations plus the known station geometry give the 6-DOF pose. Keep rotation mathematics for Unit 4.

figure.title: One 60 Hz frame of lighthouse sweeps
figure.aria: Timeline of one 16.67 ms frame: station A sweeps its X beam then its Y beam, then station B repeats, so a photodiode is hit four times per frame.

chapters.example: A headset gyroscope reports a steady yaw rate of 90° per second for 0.5 s. (a) What yaw change is recorded? (b) The gyroscope carries a bias of 0.2° per second that is never removed; how much yaw error has built up after 5 minutes? (c) A lighthouse base station sweeps its beam across a 120° fan in 4.17 ms; at what angular rate does the beam move? (d) A photodiode is hit 1.00 ms after the sweep starts; what angle is that from the start of the fan? Answer: (a) 90 × 0.5 = 45°. (b) 0.2 × 300 = 60°. (c) 120 ÷ 0.00417 = 28,777, about 28,800° per second. (d) (1.00 ÷ 4.17) × 120 = 28.8°.
chapters.trap: Drift grows with elapsed time, not with how fast the head turns, so a still headset still drifts. And gravity can fix pitch and roll but never yaw, because gravity carries no heading information.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.6 for accelerometer and gyroscope behaviour; Unit 4 for quaternions and rotation conversions.
chapters.leave: Full rotation mathematics to Unit 4; AR tracking and SLAM to Unit 6.
